{"id": "56:10/q02", "question": "Who are the forerunners, and in what do they precede others?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish comprehensive good deeds from particular acts, early faith across communities from early Muslims, precedence in time from rank, and differing named pioneers; some treat narrower identifications as examples.", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q02/p1", "position": "They are the first to believe in God and respond to the prophets, among every community or the earliest Muslims.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās say every nation contributes forerunners; al-Wāḥidī cites 9:100 for Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation. Muqātil and ʿIkrima stress immediate response when truth appears; al-Māwardī specifies Islam before Muhammad's emigration or arrival, before hope or fear could move converts. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the class continues into Muhammad's community. Al-Iṣlāḥī stresses early supporters' costly service with person and wealth and cites 57:10: pre-conquest spending and fighting ranked higher, though both groups receive good reward. Al-Sulamī differentiates prophets first in faith in God from truthful persons and martyrs first in faith in prophets. Ibn Zayd's knowledge prevailing over desire marks two Paradise groups, with desire's victory placing a person in Hell."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p2", "position": "They hasten to every good deed and all that God commands.", "reasons": "Al-Quraẓī and Ibn Kaysān make the scope comprehensive; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī prefer it because it includes the narrower examples. Ibn Kathīr says reward matches deeds, citing 3:133 and 57:22; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 35:32, 2:148, 23:61, and 57:21. Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī cite 23:61. Al-Kashshāf stresses sincere, energetic response; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes avoiding sins; Ibn ʿĀshūr says omitting the object generalizes every virtuous competition, as in 83:26. Al-Tustarī's and other specified examples can be read within this broad class, according to al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p3", "position": "They are first to Paradise and God's mercy because they first believed or obeyed in this life.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and al-Rabīʿ explicitly pair worldly response with Paradise. Al-Zajjāj, al-Jishumī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī pair obedience and good deeds with mercy and forgiveness. Al-Qummī applies Paradise to the second occurrence; al-Ṭabrisī says their model conduct earns the highest rank. Al-Dāmghānī and al-Bayḍāwī give Paradise as the goal."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p4", "position": "They hasten to mosques and to go out in God's cause.", "reasons": "ʿUthmān ibn Abī Sawda gives both actions; al-Wāḥidī describes the first ranks of worshippers and fighters. A report raised through Ibn ʿAbbās has the forerunner enter the mosque first and leave last; al-Ālūsī gives no grading. Mujāhid combines first jihad with early prayer departure."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p5", "position": "They are the earliest Companions who prayed toward both qiblas.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn's identification signals the Companions' early adherence; al-Wāḥidī connects it to Ibn ʿAbbās's early-belief view. Al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Ālūsī connect it with 9:100; the latter names early Emigrants and Helpers."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p6", "position": "They are those who were first to emigrate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says worldly precedence in migration yields precedence in the afterlife; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes the first Emigrants and Helpers and cites 9:100."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p7", "position": "They take precedence in the five daily prayers.", "reasons": "Attributed repeatedly to ʿAlī; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats it as an illustrative instance of the general meaning."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p8", "position": "They are first to repent and perform righteous works.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr cites the commands to race toward forgiveness in 3:133 and 57:21; al-Qurṭubī also cites 23:61. Al-Qushayrī adds regret for sin."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p9", "position": "They are the prophets, leaders of their religious communities.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb gives this identification. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī explain that prophets lead adherents of their religions. The Study Quran says many commentators include prophets; other views include saints, truthful persons and martyrs, while some put prophets beyond the forerunners."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p10", "position": "They are first to undertake jihad.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Ḍaḥḥāk in several sources; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows that this may be an instance of the general sense."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p11", "position": "They are the people of the Qurʾān.", "reasons": "Kaʿb says they will be crowned on Resurrection Day; al-Baghawī specifies reciters."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p12", "position": "They accept what is due, give when asked, and judge others as themselves.", "reasons": "A prophetic report is cited by al-Mahdawī and others; Ibn Kathīr's ʿĀʾisha version says they reach the Resurrection shade first. Wording varies between accepting a due right and accepting truth."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p13", "position": "They were first to acquire virtue, firm knowledge, and piety; their precedence is in rank.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī speaks of virtues and perfections. Al-Bursevī distinguishes rank from chronological priority; al-Ālūsī specifies certain knowledge and degrees of piety beyond faith. The Study Quran reports a virtue reading. Al-Qushayrī also reports people promised the highest reward who hasten to their allotted good."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p14", "position": "They were early and persistent doers of good throughout life.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shumayṭ and Shumayṭ ibn ʿAjlān contrast this group with late repenters on the right and lifelong evildoers on the left; the accounts differ slightly in the named transmitter and description of youth."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p15", "position": "They are the higher people of Paradise, including prophets, the truthful, and martyrs.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls them a smaller elite nearer God, after the right and left classes. Al-Suddī calls them people of ʿIlliyyīn; the Study Quran connects their upper heavenly residence with 83:18. Kuran Yolu says they are the leading portion of those receiving records in the right hand, citing 56:11 and 56:88; al-Sāmarrāʾī calls them creation's highest."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p16", "position": "They are spiritual knowers and devoted servants brought near by divine favor.", "reasons": "Al-Tustarī and al-Sulamī say God chose them for friendship or guardianship before their existence. Al-Jurayrī says they have no concern besides God; Abū ʿAlī al-Jawzajānī names true knowledge, sincere worship, longing and love. Al-Qushayrī includes sincerity and high aspiration; the Study Quran names an elite understanding religion's inner meaning."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p17", "position": "Joshua, the believer of Yā Sīn, and ʿAlī were the first for Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad respectively.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās names Joshua son of Nun, the believer of Yā Sīn, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; the reports say each preceded his community."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p18", "position": "Ḥizqīl, Ḥabīb al-Najjār, and ʿAlī are named as those who preceded their communities.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's reported list includes Pharaoh's believer, the Yā Sīn companion, and ʿAlī; al-Ālūsī adds that ʿAlī is best of them and cites 36:20. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as a revelation identification."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p19", "position": "Ḥizqīl, Ḥabīb al-Najjār, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar are singled out.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's report places Ḥizqīl with Moses' or Pharaoh's people and Ḥabīb with Jesus' people, then Abū Bakr and ʿUmar with Muhammad's people."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p20", "position": "Adam's slain son, Pharaoh's believer, Ḥabīb al-Najjār, and ʿAlī are four forerunners.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar identifies one pioneer in each named setting; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says al-Ṣādiq also transmits this account."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p21", "position": "They are monotheists who pass beyond both worlds through annihilation in God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says they outstrip both other groups."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p22", "position": "Abū Bakr and ʿAlī are among the foremost in belief and Paradise.", "reasons": "Muqātil singles out these two as first in belief in God and His Messenger among their communities."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p23", "position": "ʿAlī and his Shiʿa precede to Paradise and are brought near.", "reasons": "A report from Ibn ʿAbbās attributes this identification to Gabriel speaking to the Prophet; another report from ʿAlī says the verse was revealed about him."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p24", "position": "The Prophet, Salmān, Bilāl, and Ṣuhayb are the foremost of Arabs, Persians, Abyssinians, and Romans.", "reasons": "Reported as a prophetic saying, assigning one named forerunner to each people."}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p25", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar identifies his own community as the foremost and the last.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar says, 'We are the foremost, and we are the last ones.'"}, {"id": "56:10/q02/p26", "position": "They bypass the Reckoning and enter Paradise directly.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports this view, distinguishing them from right- and left-hand groups who stand for judgment."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q03", "question": "How does the repetition of al-sābiqūn work?", "turns_on": "The disputed syntax is subject and predicate, emphatic repetition with a following predicate, adjective plus predicate, or an ellipsis; the subject-predicate parse may praise renowned rank or assign different objects to each occurrence.", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q03/p1", "position": "The first al-sābiqūn is the subject and the second its predicate, acclaiming a renowned rank beyond fuller description.", "reasons": "Sībawayh's analysis is preferred by Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī prefer this over emphasis. Al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn, and others compare Abū al-Najm's 'my poetry is my poetry' to repeated renown. Al-Rāzī says their state surpasses 
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<chunk 211, part 1 of 0..5>>
knowledge; al-Qāshānī says no praise can encompass it. Al-Iṣlāḥī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say no predicate better conveys their rank. Al-Ālūsī says no different objects need be supplied. Ibn ʿĀshūr's general comments, citing al-Sakkākī, connect rhetorical analysis with Qur'anic inimitability."}, {"id": "56:10/q03/p2", "position": "The second noun emphatically repeats the first; 'those are the brought-near' supplies the predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabarī and others give this parse. Al-Kashshāf places a sound pause after the second noun and says it parallels the other groups. Al-Samīn describes the next words as a new clause in predicate position and compares 7:26. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the repetition expresses amazement. Al-Ālūsī rejects it for weakening the division and later contrast; al-Nasafī favors the predicate parse."}, {"id": "56:10/q03/p3", "position": "The second al-sābiqūn predicates a different precedence: first in faith or obedience here, then first in mercy or Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and his transmitters distinguish obedience and mercy; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn allow faith, obedience, or good works paired with Paradise or mercy. Ṣāḥib al-Murshid gives obedience/mercy and good/Paradise. Al-Ālūsī prefers the complete predicate without supplying different objects."}, {"id": "56:10/q03/p4", "position": "The second noun is an adjective modifying the first, with the predicate following.", "reasons": "Some grammarians give this parse. Abū Isḥāq allows it; Abū Ḥayyān allows it when the two words have different objects. Al-Ālūsī defends adjectival analysis by saying the definite article need not be relative here. Al-Samīn rejects a bare adjective as pointless and suggests its proponents meant emphasis."}, {"id": "56:10/q03/p5", "position": "The first noun is coordinated with the right-hand group, or stands as a separate clause after a pause.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports coordination with the preceding right-hand people before the clause 'those are the brought-near.' Al-Samīn rejects the pause-and-new-clause version because it strains coordination and requires an insertion."}, {"id": "56:10/q03/p6", "position": "Each group label serves as predicate of an omitted topic; the repeated label introduces its description.", "reasons": "Al-Irshād says the division naturally names categories before describing them; earlier descriptions preview the other groups' eventual states, while the forerunners receive description immediately. Al-Ālūsī favors this sequence. A criticism says the parse only identifies groups and leaves the two earlier questions unexplained; another analysis allows the questions to modify prior labels after an implied saying."}, {"id": "56:10/q03/p7", "position": "The phrase tacitly follows an omitted question, 'What are the forerunners?'", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī infers that question from the two preceding 'what are the companions of the right/left?' questions."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q04", "question": "What is their rank among the three groups?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q04/p1", "position": "They are the third, most excellent class, brought near above the companions of the right.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls them the third group in 56:7; Ibn Kathīr makes them a smaller elite including messengers, prophets, truthful people and martyrs. Al-Biqāʿī links them to the first two gardens in al-Raḥmān and calls them people of the heart. Kuran Yolu makes them the leading part of those given the right-hand record, citing 56:11 and 56:88. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts their highest Paradise rank with the lesser rank of the right-hand group. The Study Quran reports the highest parts of Heaven."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q05", "question": "How can the forerunners describe the soul's inner faculties?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q05/p1", "position": "The spirit races through care, the heart through guarding, and the limbs through service.", "reasons": "Al-Jurayrī pairs these with modesty, purity, and recompense as their respective gifts."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q06", "question": "What brings the forerunners near to God?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes ground nearness in prior divine gift or in recompense corresponding to the servants' deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q06/p1", "position": "Precedence in obedience and good deeds is answered by precedence in mercy, honor, and Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and al-Rabīʿ align worldly and afterlife precedence. Ibn Kathīr says recompense matches deeds, citing 3:133 and 57:22; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī pairs works with corresponding forgiveness and mercy, citing 57:21."}, {"id": "56:10/q06/p2", "position": "God's choice and gift bring them near; their attributed racing does not itself produce nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī says divine friendship was given before their existence. Al-Qāsim reasons that, though God attributes racing to servants, their act itself cannot make them near or it would truly belong to them. Al-Qushayrī reports a promised highest reward and haste toward allotted good."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q07", "question": "What is reported about the relative numbers of forerunners?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q07/p1", "position": "Earlier nations have more forerunners, while right-hand people from earlier nations and this community are equal in number.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports this from the Prophet and connects the count of right-hand people with 56:39."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q08", "question": "What is said about a forerunner's light in Paradise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q08/p1", "position": "A resident's light identifies him to those below when he leaves his Paradise dwelling.", "reasons": "A Kufan informant gives this description of a foremost, brought-near resident."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q09", "question": "How did speakers use the idea of racing to encourage people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q09/p1", "position": "They urged others to advance, while one speaker said the brought-near people win the race.", "reasons": "ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr repeated 'Go ahead, go ahead'; ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays answered a question about a race's winner by naming those brought near to God."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q10", "question": "Why are the forerunners placed after the other groups and described next?", "turns_on": "The notes explain either the delayed placement and immediate description by merit and exhortation, or the absence of an interrogative by their inexpressible rank.", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q10/p1", "position": "The best group is mentioned third so its excellent state can be described next and its merit draw attention.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says their merit warrants priority before detailing the left; al-Biqāʿī says the highest rank among the right encourages excellence while leaving the left undivided as warning. Al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say third placement leads directly into their excellent states. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds curiosity, emulation, and a deliberate unfolding of the three groups through proximity and relative priority."}, {"id": "56:10/q10/p2", "position": "Their known greatness makes an interrogative challenge unnecessary.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts the question about the right-hand companions in 56:8: people already admit they cannot grasp the forerunners' state. Ibn ʿĀshūr says repeating their name conveys honor more strongly than the exclamatory wording for the right."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q11", "question": "What kind of standing do the three groups represent?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q11/p1", "position": "The classes express moral standing by faith and deeds at Judgment, rather than physical placement before God.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī says Judgment overturns worldly standards, divides humanity in verses 1–10, and raises or abases by faith and deeds; spatial right, left, front, and back make no sense before God. Ibn Zayd distinguishes knowledge ruling desire from desire ruling knowledge; the latter leads to Hell. Al-Itqān says the examples of neglecting obligations, fulfilling them, and exceeding in good deeds illustrate rather than exhaust the classes."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q12", "question": "How does this threefold grouping connect with other Qurʾānic passages and the sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different correspondences: 35:32's moral classes, al-Raḥmān's garden levels, al-Ṣāffāt's ranking, and the sūra's judgment theme.", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q12/p1", "position": "The three groups correspond to the wrongdoers, moderate believers, and those foremost in good in another Qurʾānic division.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr associates the sūra's beginning and end with 35:32, on one reading of 'wronging oneself.' Al-Burhān and al-Itqān make the three classifications exhaustive; al-Itqān says concrete examples do not exhaust the general classes."}, {"id": "56:10/q12/p2", "position": "The three ranks continue al-Raḥmān's gradation of punishment and two levels of gardens.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls the sūra Meccan and following al-Raḥmān; he maps unbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers to its garden pairs and to this sūra's opening and closing groups, citing 55:62. Al-Biqāʿī assigns the forerunners the first two gardens. The Study Quran says al-Wāqiʿa completes al-Raḥmān's Paradise/Hell contrast."}, {"id": "56:10/q12/p3", "position": "The sūra's movement toward judgment organizes the fate of all three classes.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī says verses 1–10 establish Judgment and its threefold evaluation; verse 3's raising and lowering becomes the three groups. The Study Quran identifies their afterlife fates as the sūra's central theme."}, {"id": "56:10/q12/p4", "position": "The few forerunners here occupy a higher degree than other servants mentioned in al-Ṣāffāt.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the lower degree of servants in 37:40 with the forerunners' highest ranks in Paradise."}]}

 three classes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q13/p1", "position": "Each person is joined with peers who did like deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr reports the Prophet's explanation of the three classes; Ibn Kathīr connects it to souls paired in 81:7."}]}
{"id": "56:10/q14", "question": "What report compares righteous humans with angels?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:10/q14/p1", "position": "God refuses angels' request for the Hereafter in place of Adam's children's worldly goods and does not equate them with righteous offspring of one created by His hand.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr recounts three appeals and God's contrast with one created by 'Be,' then recites these verses. Al-Dārimī's version specifies righteous offspring and appears in Refutation of the Jahmiyya."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q01", "question": "Who are 'those' identified as the brought-near?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding category names every person who leads in good, a particular early cohort, or named persons; the reports give different identifications.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q01/p1", "position": "The foremost people, understood broadly as those who lead in faith, obedience, and good deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi and al-Tabataba'i identify the demonstrative with the preceding forerunners (56:10). Al-Kalbi says they raced to faith in life and will race to Paradise; Ibn Kathir says recompense matches their haste toward commanded good, citing 3:133 and 57:22, and accepts the several accounts together. Ibn Atiyya, as reported by Kur'an Yolu, includes all who lead in good and avoid evil, hence lead in afterlife felicity. The Study Quran reports the same basic identification."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p2", "position": "The first believers in their respective prophets and the near ones of each community.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi presents this as another possibility."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p3", "position": "Prophets and messengers, with the truthful and martyrs among their followers also included.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas compares the brought-near to prophets and messengers. Al-Tustari says prophets were foremost in God, and the truthful and martyrs among Companions and others were foremost in the prophets."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p4", "position": "The early, persistent doers of good, distinguished from later penitents and persistent sinners.", "reasons": "The account in al-Kashshaf makes late repenters people of the right and persistent youthful evildoers people of the left. Shumayt ibn Ajlan, reported by al-Qurtubi, describes the same three endings: early sustained goodness, repentance after sin, and persistence in sin."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p5", "position": "Ali and his Shi'a, who precede to Paradise.", "reasons": "In Ibn Abbas's report, Gabriel identifies the verse this way to the Prophet and says they are brought near through God's honor."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p6", "position": "Ali ibn Abi Talib specifically.", "reasons": "A report transmitted from Ali in al-Uyun says the words were revealed concerning him."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p7", "position": "The first believers.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this among narrower identifications offered by unnamed commentators."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p8", "position": "The earliest emigrants.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this among narrower identifications offered by unnamed commentators."}, {"id": "56:11/q01/p9", "position": "Companions who prayed toward both qiblas.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports this among narrower identifications offered by unnamed commentators."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q02", "question": "What does the distant demonstrative 'those' convey?", "turns_on": "The notes explain different rhetorical effects of the demonstrative without rejecting either one.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q02/p1", "position": "It marks the forerunners' exalted rank despite their being the nearby antecedent.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi notes that the distant form points back to the forerunners while signaling elevation."}, {"id": "56:11/q02/p2", "position": "It presents their previously named foremost quality as the reason they deserve the predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares the demonstrative in 2:5."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q03", "question": "How is 'those are the brought-near' parsed in its context?", "turns_on": "The status of the repeated 'forerunners,' whether this clause predicates an earlier subject or resumes the exposition, and whether the demonstrative can form an adjective.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q03/p1", "position": "It is the predicate after the first 'forerunners' as subject and the second as emphatic repetition or adjective.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, al-Zajjaj, Abu Ishaq as reported by al-Nahhas, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Tabataba'i transmit the emphatic analysis. Al-Kashshaf makes the phrase the predicate and places the sound pause after the second 'forerunners,' paralleling the other groups. Ibn Atiyya allows it as predicate on the adjective analysis. Al-Alusi rejects the emphatic parse because it weakens the division, rhetoric, and ensuing contrast."}, {"id": "56:11/q03/p2", "position": "It is a fresh subject-predicate sentence that explains the forerunners' outcome.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi calls it an explanatory resumption; Ibn Ashur makes it the answer to the question raised by praise of the foremost, namely their reward. Al-Tabataba'i prefers this parse because division into three groups is followed by each outcome. Ibn Atiyya calls 'those' subject and 'brought-near' predicate. Al-Nahhas permits apposition or a second predicate instead of an adjective. Al-Alusi reports an adjective analysis of preceding group labels after an implied saying, then a resumed explanatory clause; he answers the objection about deleting a relative pronoun by denying that al- is relative here when no new occurrence is indicated."}, {"id": "56:11/q03/p3", "position": "The second 'forerunners' is predicate of the first; this verse then describes them.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi explain that precedence in obedience leads to precedence in God's mercy. Abu Ishaq as reported by al-Nahhas offers the same alternative. Al-Nasafi favors the first 'forerunners' as predicate over emphatic repetition. Abu Hayyan also reports a distinction between preceding in faith and preceding to Paradise, with the second term predicate or adjective and a later predicate."}, {"id": "56:11/q03/p4", "position": "The prior group labels are predicates of omitted topics; 'the forerunners' repeats for grandeur, then 'those' begins a second topic or apposition and 'brought-near' predicates it.", "reasons": "Al-Irshad, reported by al-Alusi, says the expected step after dividing humanity is to name each category, then describe it. The first two groups' descriptions are parenthetical previews, while the forerunners receive their description immediately. Al-Alusi prefers this as more natural than making the initial point a judgment about the groups; he reports the objection that it identifies groups without detailing their states and leaves unexplained why two questions are omitted from the detailed account."}, {"id": "56:11/q03/p5", "position": "'Those' is the subject and 'in Gardens of Bliss' in the next verse is its predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports this alternative analysis."}, {"id": "56:11/q03/p6", "position": "The phrase is an adjective modifying the forerunners.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas argues against this: demonstratives are more definite than nouns with alif-lam, so he allows apposition or a second predicate instead."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q04", "question": "What does being 'brought-near' mean, and near to what?", "turns_on": "The notes variously specify God and His favor, Paradise, the Throne, or inward states as the referent or sense of nearness; al-Qushayri and Ibn Ashur explicitly explain nonspatial nearness.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q04/p1", "position": "They are near God in honor, favor, and exalted standing.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives rank and excellence; al-Tustari adds stations of intimacy. Al-Tha'labi places them near God in Gardens of Bliss. Al-Wahidi's brief commentary names God's honor, and his specialists in meaning name abundant recompense and great honor. Al-Baghawi simply names nearness to God. Al-Tabrisi joins mercy, highest ranks, reward, and honor. Al-Qushayri denies spatial distance: selves are near Paradise, hearts near the Real and gnosis, spirits in witnessing, while God transcends near and far. Al-Alusi names standing with God. Elmalili gives the highest rank in His presence. Ibn Ashur treats nearness figuratively as the care accorded a beloved person, citing the sacred hadith about supererogatory worship, divine love, hearing, sight, hand, and foot. Al-Tabataba'i says God grants special honor, forgiveness, and mercy as causes of misery fall away, citing 83:20-21, 27-28. The Study Quran reports nearness to God Himself."}, {"id": "56:11/q04/p2", "position": "Their elevated Paradise ranks are near the Divine Throne.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf locates their high ranks near the Throne. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi adds the shade of the Throne and divine presence. Abu Hayyan says 'those' indicates raised Paradise stations near the Throne. Bursevi adds purified souls ascending to precincts of holiness. Al-Alusi and the Study Quran report the Throne interpretation."}, {"id": "56:11/q04/p3", "position": "They are brought near within the Gardens of Bliss or the Garden of Eden.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi in al-Wahidi names Eden as their destination; Ibn Atiyya says nearness to God is in Eden. Al-Baydawi links nearness to raised ranks in Gardens of Bliss. The Study Quran reports Gardens of Bliss; Ibn Kathir includes gardens in his inclusive account. reasons": "Al-Razi says the people of the right are still receiving their books, referring to 56:8."}, {"id": "56:11/q04/p5", "position": "They continually ascend in Paradise, so they remain above the others even as those others approach.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says they reach the highest levels as the others reach the houris, referring to 56:8."}, {"id": "56:11/q04/p6", "position": "They are brought near in their allotted shares and spiritual states.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports this alternative while insisting the Real remains beyond even their purified states."}, {"id": "56:11/q04/p7", "position": "They have realized Real existence after annihilation.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani gives this inward interpretation of the brought-near."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q05", "question": "Why are they called 'brought-near' rather than people who draw near?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q05/p1", "position": "The passive form marks God's prior choice and gracious act of bringing them close.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says God's drawing near precedes their effort and marks the station of union. Al-Biqa'i says without God's choice and drawing near they would not have become forerunners. Ibn Ashur says muqarrab is stronger than qarib because its form implies selection and favor."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q06", "question": "What does the omitted complement of 'brought-near' imply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q06/p1", "position": "God's care and favor are understood, while omitted time and place extend nearness to life here and the hereafter.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the object is obvious, and the lack of temporal and spatial restriction generalizes the description."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q07", "question": "How does this rank compare with other ranks?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q07/p1", "position": "It is the highest human rank, though others may possess lesser nearness.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls it the highest human afterlife rank. Al-Tabataba'i ties the highest blessed rank to the forerunners in 56:10. Elmalili gives the highest station; Samarra'i calls them highest in creation against the people of the right. Islahi says pioneer status brings first reward and nearest position, with paradises matching ranks. Al-Tabrisi names the highest ranks."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q08", "question": "What conduct or spiritual state leads to this rank?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize deeds and faith, complete servitude or freedom from self-interest, and God's prior choosing; Ibn Kathir accepts multiple accounts of the forerunners together.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q08/p1", "position": "Precedence in faith, obedience, and sustained good works leads to precedence in the next life.", "reasons": "Al-Tustari names worldly precedence in faith; al-Kalbi says they race to faith and then Paradise. Al-Zajjaj, repeated by al-Qurtubi, connects precedence in obedience with God's mercy. Al-Kashshaf and Shumayt distinguish persistent early goodness from later repentance and continued evil. Ibn Kathir holds that racing to commanded good earns first honor because recompense matches deeds (3:133; 57:22). Al-Itqan treats forerunners exceeding in good as an example of a general category, alongside duty-neglecting unjust and duty-performing middle people, not an exhaustive definition. Kur'an Yolu's Ibn Atiyya includes leading in good and avoiding evil. Al-Tabataba'i says deeds remove causes of deprivation and open divine mercy."}, {"id": "56:11/q08/p2", "position": "Complete servitude is required for the highest rank.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i infers this from the link between the brought-near and forerunners in 56:10."}, {"id": "56:11/q08/p3", "position": "They are freed from self-interest and treat every worldly and religious duty as God's right.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i reports al-Razi's account: both divine and human rights become God's rights; he distinguishes those absorbed in awe from others entrusted with easier service."}, {"id": "56:11/q08/p4", "position": "God's choice and prior drawing near enables their precedence.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says they could not be forerunners without God's act; al-Qushayri says divine drawing near precedes their own effort."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q09", "question": "What does nearness to God signify beyond physical distance?", "turns_on": "Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes a servant's approach to divine mercy from God's encompassing nearness to everything.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q09/p1", "position": "For servants it is figurative participation in God's favor, mercy, care, and spiritual witnessing.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says their selves are near Paradise, hearts near the Real and gnosis, and spirits in witnessing, while God transcends nearness, distance, separation, and union. Ibn Ashur compares divine care to treatment of a loved person and cites the sacred hadith about supererogatory worship, divine love, and God becoming the servant's hearing, sight, hand, and foot. Al-Tabataba'i traces the word from spatial bodies to time, comparison, and nonphysical realities; good deeds remove misery and bring a servant into mercy, while God grants honor and forgiveness."}, {"id": "56:11/q09/p2", "position": "God's own nearness means His encompassing of all things, even being nearer to a thing than it is to itself.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i cites 2:186, 56:85, and 50:16, after tracing extension of spatial language to nonphysical realities."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q10", "question": "Are earlier brought-near people more excellent than later ones?", "turns_on": "Whether earlier numerical prevalence entails superior quality, given the harder conditions faced by later believers.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q10/p1", "position": "Greater numbers of brought-near people in earlier times do not mean greater quality.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports Ibn Ajibah's reading of the larger earlier cohort."}, {"id": "56:11/q10/p2", "position": "Some people near the end of time may be higher in degree because they strive amid widespread heedlessness.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports that late believers may earn a rank earlier people lacked despite fewer supports; it also quotes the Prophet's comparison: omitting one tenth of commands in the Companions' time brought ruin, while later fulfilling one tenth brings salvation, with no grading stated."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q11", "question": "What report illustrates the visible status of a foremost resident in Paradise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q11/p1", "position": "When such a resident leaves his Paradise dwelling, his light identifies him to people below.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi reports this from a Kufan informant, and al-Qurtubi transmits the same account."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q12", "question": "What does the report about angels and Adam's children say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q12/p1", "position": "After three angelic appeals for the Hereafter, God refused to equate righteous descendants of Adam, created by His hand, with beings made by 'Be.'", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports Abdullah ibn Amr: angels contrasted human worldly food, drink, and marriage with their own condition, then Abdullah recited these verses. He also cites al-Darimi's version in Refutation of the Jahmiyya, which specifies righteous offspring."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q13", "question": "What Prophetic report gives an instance of people who precede?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q13/p1", "position": "The foremost enter the mosque first and leave it last.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this Prophetic saying through Ibn Abbas."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q14", "question": "How does this verse develop the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "The notes explain the ordering through outcome exposition, literary distribution, and the foremost group's merit.", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q14/p1", "position": "It begins the account of the three groups' outcomes and opens the foremost group's reward.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i says these verses begin Resurrection outcomes for each class. Ibn Ashur calls the brought-near clause an explanatory answer to the praise-induced question about reward, and the distribution a nashr ba'd al-laff arranged by proximity of meaning and relative priority. Islahi says 56:11-26 describes the foremost's Paradise gifts and qualifying character; he adds that leaders and pioneers are rewarded first."}, {"id": "56:11/q14/p2", "position": "The forerunners are explained before the people of the left because their merit deserves priority.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says the discourse first names those affected by the warnings and then gives the forerunners priority in exposition."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q15", "question": "How does this group connect this sura with al-Rahman?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q15/p1", "position": "Al-Rahman's two pairs of gardens distinguish lower and higher believers, matching the three groups in this sura.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says this Meccan sura follows al-Rahman, which pairs sinners' punishment with believers' bliss. The lower pair in 55:62 yields unbelievers, lower-ranking believers, and superior believers, matching the three groups at this sura's opening and the companions of the right and deniers at its close."}]}
{"id": "56:11/q16", "question": "What added degree does this wording express beside al-Saffat?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:11/q16/p1", "position": "Being brought near in al-Waqi'a adds a degree beyond being honored in al-Saffat.", "reasons": "Samarrāʾī makes this comparison."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q01", "question": "What does the pronoun in 'indeed it' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the unexpressed antecedent is the familiar revelation as a whole or the preceding discourse.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q01/p1"

{"id": "56:77/q02", "question": "What does the name Qur'an mean and how is it derived?", "turns_on": "Whether it is a proper name or derived, and, if derived, which root and morphological account explain its sense and hamza.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q02/p1", "position": "A recitation or recited speech, derived from reading; a verbal noun can name what is read.", "reasons": "Razi compares verbal noun used for object in 13:31 and 31:11; al-Lihyani calls it a verbal noun like ghufran; Ibn Ashur stresses repeated reading and contemplation and cites 10:61; Study Quran gives the linguistic sense 'noble recitation'; Burhan also describes sequential recitation."}, {"id": "56:77/q02/p2", "position": "A proper, non-derived name for God's particular revelation, pronounced without hamza.", "reasons": "Isma'il ibn Qustantine argues that derivation from reading would make every recited text a Qur'an; al-Shafi'i reportedly hamzated qara'tu but not Quran and compared its proper-name status to Torah and Gospel; al-Wahidi transmits his view; al-Suyuti chooses it, while Alusi criticizes that as unargued deference and prefers al-Zajjaj."}, {"id": "56:77/q02/p3", "position": "Derived from qar', gathering or collecting.", "reasons": "Al-Jawhari gives the root; Abu Ubayd says it gathers suras; al-Raghib says it gathers fruits of earlier scriptures but cautions that not every collection is called Quran, perhaps a point about usage; al-Harawi says anything gathered has been read; al-Zajjaj compares collecting water in a basin and takes the hamza as original, with its omission due to lightening; Alusi accepts this analysis on the common hamzated form."}, {"id": "56:77/q02/p4", "position": "Derived from joining together its suras, verses and letters.", "reasons": "Al-Ash'ari compares qiran joining pilgrimage rites; Alusi says the proposed n is original and there is no hamza."}, {"id": "56:77/q02/p5", "position": "Derived from qara'in, because its verses confirm and resemble one another.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Qurtubi and al-Farra; this treats n as radical and the form as unhamzated. Al-Zajjaj calls the derivation mistaken, explaining missing hamza as lightening and vowel transfer; al-Farisi notes that analysis."}, {"id": "56:77/q02/p6", "position": "A noun for what is recited, rather than a verbal noun transferred to its object.", "reasons": "Razi compares qurban for what is offered and hulwan for what is given or tasted; he says this validates jurists' al-jubran for what effects compensation."}, {"id": "56:77/q02/p7", "position": "Derived from bringing forth or making something manifest and articulate.", "reasons": "A later scholar cites 75:17 to distinguish gathering from Quran; Qutrub compares the reciter bringing it out of his mouth to an expression about a she-camel bringing forth a fetal membrane."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q03", "question": "How is the hamza of Qur'an read and explained?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronounced or lightened hamza reflects the word's derivation or a regional reading practice.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q03/p1", "position": "The hamza is original and pronounced; omission is phonetic lightening with its vowel moved to the preceding consonant.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj rejects an unhamzated derivation; al-Farisi records the vowel-transfer explanation. Alusi favors it because six of seven readers pronounce hamza and the hamzated form is common."}, {"id": "56:77/q03/p2", "position": "The hamza is omitted or softened in the reading qurān.", "reasons": "Al-Bayhaqi reports al-Shafi'i's unhamzated Quran despite his hamzated qara'tu; al-Wahidi and al-Suyuti report Ibn Kathir's reading; Qiraat-ER calls dropping or softening it standard Hijazi practice."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q04", "question": "Why call the revelation a Qur'an here?", "turns_on": "Whether the disputed assertion is its reception as a lasting recitation or the entire noble description.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q04/p1", "position": "Calling it Qur'an establishes received, enduring recitation and rebuts the claim that Muhammad invented it.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this: Muhammad received and recited it, and it will be recited perpetually in this life and the next; he separately says the designation counters self-composition."}, {"id": "56:77/q04/p2", "position": "The deniers rejected the full characterization 'noble Qur'an,' not the bare fact that it could be recited.", "reasons": "Razi reports this as an alternative answer to why the descriptive name is asserted."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q05", "question": "What makes the Qur'an karīm, or noble?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of nobility the adjective foregrounds: intrinsic excellence, benefit, divine honor, moral guidance, transmission, protection, or theological status.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q05/p1", "position": "It possesses excellent, praiseworthy qualities and is free of baseness or defect.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take the adjective as praise excluding defects; Ibn al-Jawzi and Study Quran call it comprehensive of praised qualities; Qushayri excludes baseness; Razi defines true nobility by pure origin and manifest excellence, with eloquent wording and sound meaning, and rejects reducing it to giving; Ibn Ashur says its comprehensive guidance, proof, refutation, clarity, concision, eloquence and sound surpass earlier books, citing 27:29. Others call it excellent, beautiful, precious, or pleasing among books."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p2", "position": "It gives abundant benefit, guidance, knowledge, reward, and good for this life and the next.", "reasons": "Mawardi adds benefit to memorizer and reciter; Tabarsi cites proofs leading to truth and reward for reciting and acting; Razi says jurists, sages and writers each find what they need and its exact words are easy to memorize; Baydawi, al-Tibi, Bursevi and Elmalili point to foundational knowledge for both lives. Alusi reports a dispute whether generosity for benefit is metaphorical (al-Tibi) or literal under a broad sense of praiseworthy qualities. Alusi also reports an honor-in-God's-sight sense but calls its implied preposition unnecessary. Qurtubi describes healing for believers' hearts."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p3", "position": "God has honored and exalted it as His speech and revelation.", "reasons": "Maqatil explicitly attributes its exaltation to God; believers and heaven's people honor their Lord's speech and revelation (Qurtubi); Bag hawi and Tabarsi cite its being God's speech; al-Kashshaf and others give 'honored by God.' Alusi says this reading returns to the preceding excellence sense and needs an unnecessary implied preposition."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p4", "position": "It directs people to noble character, lofty aims and virtuous deeds.", "reasons": "Sulami and Bursevi state this directly; Mawardi includes noble character and lofty matters; Qushayri says it guides noble character; Qurtubi speaks of noble character and weighty meanings; Kuranyolu includes morals among its riches."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p5", "position": "It came from the Noble Lord through noble messengers to the noblest human recipient.", "reasons": "Sulami describes a noble intermediary and noblest creature; Qushayri specifies generous Lord, noble Messenger and angel; Biqai specifies highest King, Holy Spirit, best of creation, eloquent Arabic and inimitability; Bursevi repeats the transmission chain."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p6", "position": "It confers honor on its memorizer and reciter.", "reasons": "Mawardi says both are honored; Qurtubi says it honors the memorizer and magnifies the reciter."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p7", "position": "It is noble through protection, inimitability, and sublime contents.", "reasons": "Tabarsi adds immunity from alteration, inimitability, rulings and admonitions; Kuranyolu says the final perfected book is protected from falsehood and full of proof, knowledge and wisdom; Biqai calls its Arabic form inimitable; Kashshaf notes the protected book's inaccessibility to all but purified angels if it means the Preserved Tablet."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p8", "position": "It remains fresh through every repetition.", "reasons": "Razi contrasts ordinary speech, which grows stale, and says even angels who knew it before Muhammad hear it with a new listener's delight."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p9", "position": "Its ease overcomes its difficulty.", "reasons": "Thalabi reports this explanation of generosity."}, {"id": "56:77/q05/p10", "position": "It is uncreated.", "reasons": "Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya al-Kinani states this; Qushayri draws it from nobility's exclusion of baseness; Qurtubi reports it as a gloss of karim."}]}

Tabarsi distinguishes the eternal attribute of God as noble giver from the Qur'an's plentiful benefits; Burhan says God's speech was made heard and understood by Gabriel without specifying modality. {"id": "56:77/q07", "question": "What is the object and force of the preceding oath?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath directly authenticates the Qur'an or principally asserts the earlier proofs of monotheism and resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q07/p1", "position": "The oath affirms that the revelation to Muhammad is a noble Qur'an.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya identifies the Qur'an as the object; Qurtubi calls this the oath's answer against sorcery, soothsaying and fabrication; Ibn Kathir says the tremendous oath magnifies the great book. Sa'id ibn Jubayr takes la as extra; other exegetes take it as a meaningful response to denial, citing Aisha's oath usage; Arabists quoted by al-Tabari read 'it is not as you claim' before a fresh oath. Alusi says the description confirms and glorifies the preceding oath."}, {"id": "56:77/q07/p2", "position": "The oath's more apparent object is divine oneness and resurrection.", "reasons": "Razi prefers these themes, which the preceding discourse has argued for."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q08", "question": "How does the intervening conditional affect the oath and this description?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q08/p1", "position": "It is a parenthetical interruption between connected elements, magnifying the oath and the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Nasafi and Alusi place 'if you only knew' between noun and adjective; Alusi says its unexpressed answer denies knowledge or implies reverence and action. Suyuti places the interruption between oath and description and says it signals grandeur beyond their knowledge; Qudama defines i'tirad as syntactically ungoverned insertion for a purpose beyond clearing ambiguity, and al-Tibi says unexpected useful meaning makes it effective. Zarkashi rejects a restriction on parentheticals: they may occur with or without waw, as in this passage and 34:31."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q09", "question": "What does the affirmation teach about the Qur'an's origin and authority?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q09/p1", "position": "It is God's exalted revelation to Muhammad, immune to charges of magic, soothsaying or human invention.", "reasons": "Qurtubi calls it praiseworthy revelation and a miracle; Razi frames the denial as poetry or magic and the rebuttal as received recitation; Alusi stresses revealed rather than composed. Islahi says the oath testifies to divine origin, the protected book and access only by pure near angels, never jinn or devils; the section warns Quraysh against ignoring the message. Tabatabai cites other verses about a guarded tablet, exalted wise source and protected book, with enduring unchanging realities beneath the meanings."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q10", "question": "How does this affirmation connect with the sura's argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q10/p1", "position": "After proofs of oneness and resurrection, the oath establishes the divine Qur'an that teaches those truths.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says deniers reject the truths by denying the Qur'an, so the proofs come first and the revelation's source is affirmed afterward; Razi describes the preceding discussion as monotheism, resurrection and their proofs; Islahi treats verses 75–96 as declaring the Qur'an's exalted and protected status, with a warning to Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q11", "question": "What inward reading is given to the noble Qur'an and its hidden book?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q11/p1", "position": "It is exalted, ancient, comprehensive knowledge deposited as Qur'anic intellect in the Prophet's heart.", "reasons": "Qashani makes the hidden book the Prophet's heart, beyond the senses except to purified angels."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q12", "question": "How many and which broad names does the Qur'an bear?", "turns_on": "Whether the names are counted individually or reduced to two fundamental names.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q12/p1", "position": "It bears many names and descriptions, with catalogues ranging beyond fifty.", "reasons": "Zarkashi reports al-Harali's more than ninety and Qadi Abu al-Ma'ali's fifty-five, including Book, Qur'an, Speech, Light, Guidance, Mercy, Criterion and Healing (44:2, 9:6, 4:174, 31:3, 10:58, 25:1, 17:82); his further catalogue includes admonition, reminder, noble, exalted, wisdom, wise, guardian, blessed and God's rope (10:57, 21:50, 56:77, 43:4, 54:5, 10:1, 5:48, 38:29, 3:103). Suyuti lists firmest handhold, truth, justice, command, herald, glad tidings, glorious, Psalms, bearer of good news and warning, mighty, proclamation and stories, citing 2:256, 31:22, 39:33, 6:115, 65:5, 3:193, 2:97, 27:2, 85:21, 21:105, 41:3–4, 41:41, 14:52, 12:3 and 80:13–14; Alusi reports Shidla's fifty-five and Suyuti's discussion."}, {"id": "56:77/q12/p2", "position": "The many names ultimately reduce to Qur'an and Furqan.", "reasons": "Alusi compares this reduction to divine names returning to attributes of beauty and majesty."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q13", "question": "What do the Qur'an's other titles say about it?", "turns_on": "The titles point to different functions and qualities rather than a single disputed etymology.", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q13/p1", "position": "It clarifies, guides and distinguishes truth from falsehood.", "reasons": "Zarkashi explains guidance, clarification, manifest and Furqan; Furqan also distinguishes believers from unbelievers and hypocrites and explains Umar's title al-Faruq. Suyuti explains al-mubin similarly; 'guardian' testifies that earlier scriptures came from God and 'confirming' affirms prophets or scriptures before alteration."}, {"id": "56:77/q13/p2", "position": "It conveys remembrance, warning, glad tidings and the prophetic message.", "reasons": "Zarkashi says remembrance or dhikr recounts past nations and admonishes; dhikra recalls God's oneness on which believers were created; stories recount earlier peoples; bearer of glad tidings and warner promises Paradise and warns of Fire; message and balagh express the Prophet's delivery and informing people. Wahy is swift, secret communication by speech to prophets or angels, inspiration to bees, or ants' signs."}, {"id": "56:77/q13/p3", "position": "Its titles point to divine benefit, healing, mercy, light and wise rule.", "reasons": "Zarkashi says kalam impresses a new benefit on the listener's mind; light clarifies subtle lawful and unlawful matters; healing cures unbelief through faith and ignorance through learning and practice; understanding brings mercy; wise verses establish lawful and unlawful rulings, defy imitation and restrain indecency through practice."}, {"id": "56:77/q13/p4", "position": "Its titles mark its preservation, inimitability and descent from God.", "reasons": "Zarkashi says aziz means imitators cannot match its reports and recitation in striking composition (17:88), while another account says a reciter who practices it is not humiliated; Razi says those who turn from it retain nothing, unlike forgotten books. Majid means noble and free of addition, loss and alteration; the Qur'an is miraculous; tanzil means God made Gabriel hear and understand His speech as He willed, without modality, and Gabriel conveyed it. As hakim it also defies imitation."}, {"id": "56:77/q13/p5", "position": "As hakim it makes a devoted reader independent of other sciences.", "reasons": "Razi states this distinct effect of engaging with the Qur'an wholeheartedly."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q14", "question": "What is said about the Qur'an's opening letters?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q14/p1", "position": "Each sura's opening letters suit the frequency of letters in that sura's vocabulary.", "reasons": "Zarkashi says that compared with similarly sized suras, words made from a sura's opening letters recur more often, making another opening unsuitable."}]}
{"id": "56:77/q15", "question": "What examples are given of hidden insight drawn from Qur'anic verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:77/q15/p1", "position": "Ibn Barjan's reading of 30:2–4 was used to predict Jerusalem's conquest after Aleppo.", "reasons": "Ibn Khallikan reports that after Saladin took Aleppo in Safar, judge Muhyi al-Din recited a poem predicting Jerusalem's conquest in Rajab; the judge cited Ibn Barjan's tafsir, which the historian later found along with its calculation."}, {"id": "56:77/q15/p2", "position": "Ibn al-Kamal inferred Sultan Selim's conquest of Egypt from 21:105.", "reasons": "Alusi gives this as a well-known example."}, {"id": "56:77/q15/p3", "position": "Sufi masters may possess valid insights beyond a reader's present understanding.", "reasons": "Alusi urges fairness toward masters of the Muhammadan spiritual circle, suspicion of one's own limitations, and compares trusting their perception to trusting those who sighted the crescent."}]}
